note.text:
Characters (letters, digits, punctuation, spaces) are stored as numbers, using a code that both computers agree on.
ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) gives each character a number from 0 to 127 (7 bits, usually stored in one byte):
• “A” = 65, “B” = 66, … “Z” = 90;
• “a” = 97, “b” = 98, … (each small letter is 32 more than its capital);
• “0” = 48, “1” = 49, … “9” = 57; a space = 32.
Unicode extends this to every writing system and to emoji (é, ç, Arabic, Chinese, 😀), using up to 4 bytes per character.
Text size: in ASCII each character takes one byte, so “HELLO” takes 5 bytes.

worked_example.problem: Write the ASCII codes of the word {w}.

cards.idea: ASCII gives each character a number: “A” is {asciiOf('A')}, “a” is {asciiOf('a')}.
A small letter's code is {d} more than its capital's.
In ASCII each character takes one byte; Unicode covers all languages and emoji.

check.prompt: In ASCII, how many bytes does the text “{T}” take (spaces count too)?

misconceptions.explain: That is in bits; one character is one byte.

solution: Each character, including spaces, takes one byte.

questions.prompt: The ASCII code of “A” is {asciiOf('A')}. What is the ASCII code of “{c}”?

misconceptions.explain: That is its place in the alphabet; add it to 64.

solution: The capitals follow in order from “A” = {asciiOf('A')}.

questions.prompt: The ASCII code of “{C}” is {asciiOf(C)}. What is the code of the small letter “{lowerAll(C)}”?

misconceptions.explain: Capitals and small letters have different codes.

solution: Small letters are {d} more than their capitals.

questions.prompt: Which character has the ASCII code {asciiOf(c)}?

misconceptions.explain: Capitals and small letters differ by 32.

solution: Each character, including spaces, takes one byte.
